cards.front: Is a Java 2-D array one contiguous block of memory like a C or Fortran matrix?
cards.back: No — the outer array is contiguous and holds references; every row is its own block
cards.extra: dev.java draws the contrast explicitly: in C and Fortran a bidimensional array is a contiguous zone of memory reached by pointer arithmetic, while in Java only each individual array is contiguous. The 2-D array itself is an array of references.

cards.front: May the rows of a Java 2-D array have different lengths?
cards.back: Yes — such arrays are called irregular or jagged
cards.extra: Because each row is an independent array object, nothing forces equal widths: rows of 1, 2 and 3 elements in one int[3][] are legal and print as a triangle. A contiguous rectangular block could not represent that shape at all.

cards.front: After int[][] grid = new int[3][];, what does grid[0] hold?
cards.back: null — no row array has been allocated yet
cards.extra: The outer array contributes three reference slots, and the default value of any reference type is null. grid[0][0] therefore throws NullPointerException until grid[0] = new int[n]; has run.
